2882.dq: There is limited but solid evidence for a synchronic rule in Palaic whereby the word accent shifts one syllable to the right with the addition of an enclitic (cf. the similar rule in Latin)
2882.prule: No positional rule. Palaic has a word accent (Melchert 1993 §9: 'an element of stress as well as pitch') whose position is lexically specified: Melchert writes it into underlying stem forms (/ħáran-/ 'eagle', root-accented) and derives surface vowel length from it (all accented vowels in open syllables lengthen; /a/ and /e/ also in accented closed syllables). The only positional process stated is a synchronic rightward shift by one syllable when an enclitic is added (gen. sg. [ħá:ranas] vs. nom. sg. [ħará:s] in ḫarāš=kuwar). Accent position is inferred entirely from cuneiform plene spellings.

2883.prule: One primary stress per (non-compound) word, treated as phonemic, i.e. lexically specified: it falls on either the final or the penultimate syllable and the choice is not derivable from the surface form (Josephs 1997 Note 18: 'in many cases it is impossible to predict which syllable of a given Palauan word will be the stressed one'; the Josephs dictionaries mark stress on every multisyllabic entry). No rhythmic/alternating pattern. Later first-hand sources differ: Wilson 1972:39 'an irregular phenomenon of secondary stress which generally occurs two or three syllables before the penult', not analysed; Josephs 1975:20 and 1997:27 recognise only one stressed syllable per word ('all the others will be unstressed').

2884.prule: Lexical (contrastive) word stress inherited from the Spanish etymon: every lexical word has exactly one stressed syllable, the one stressed in the corresponding Spanish word; most words are paroxytonic, but oxytones exist and stress position distinguishes words (kusína 'kitchen' vs kusiná 'to cook'; Lipski 2010: mína/miná, cása/casá). 2884.tone: The paper's subject is intonation. It finds a level H tone on every stressed syllable in declaratives and interrogatives, nuclear and prenuclear, with L on posttonics and little declination ('The stressed syllable is high for most of its duration, and there is a low tone on the posttonic', p. 9); phrase-final H may stay level (no L%) or downstep to M. The authors consider and reject a tone-language analysis: one culminative, obligatory H per lexical word, no toneless lexical words, no lexical pitch-accent contrast of the Papiamentu/Swedish type; they agree with Patiño (1983, 2002) that Palenquero is 'an accentual language, rather than... a language with lexical tone', while 'closer to being a tonal-accent language' than English or Spanish (Moñino: 'tonal-accentual system'). Bickerton & Escalante 1970's 'high tone rather than stress' claim is reported and set aside. APiCS survey ch. 48 (Schwegler): 'Today, Palenquero is clearly not a tone language'.

2887.heavy: Three-way distinction: 'monomoraic light syllables, bimoraic heavy syllables, and trimoraic superheavy syllables' (p. 84); fn. 3 'L=light syllable, H=heavy syllable, S=superheavy syllable'. From the examples and ex. (1)/(7): L = (C)V (pɛ in pɛ́.laa, one mora); H = (C)VV or (C)VC (laa, kan, mee, kal); S = (C)VVC or (C)VCC (dɔɔl, aadʒ, maaɽ, buudʒ, tʃaaɽ, betʃtʃʰ). Both long vowels and codas add a mora.
2887.dflt: Not stated for all-light words: the 'exhaustive' lists (4)-(5) contain no LL or LLL pattern and monosyllables are 'minimally bimoraic'. With no superheavy: disyllables stress the initial (ĹH, H́H); trisyllables stress a heavy penult (LH́H, HH́H) else the antepenult (ĹLH, H́LH).
2887.prule: Single, non-contrastive, entirely predictable main stress placed by syllable weight on a three-way scale L (monomoraic) < H (bimoraic) < S (superheavy, trimoraic). Disyllables (rules 6, p. 86): stress the leftmost superheavy syllable if there is one (ŚH, ŚS, LŚ, HŚ -- final stress only when the final is S and the initial is not); otherwise the final mora is extrametrical and the head of the leftmost foot is stressed, i.e. initial (ĹH, H́H). Trisyllables (rules 9, p. 87): a final superheavy syllable is extrametrical; moraic trochees are built right-to-left and stress falls on the head of the second foot from the right edge, or on a degenerate foot in that position. In the attested patterns: with a final S the antepenult is stressed whatever the weight of the penult (H́HS, ĹHS); with a final H the penult is stressed when it is H or S (HH́H, LH́H, LŚH, HŚH) and the antepenult when the penult is L (ĹLH, H́LH). OT generalization (p. 92): moraic trochees built right-to-left, construction stops at the first stress-able foot, stress on the leftmost foot; superheavies attract stress; final stress avoided (NONFINALITY) except a final S in disyllables. Words of four or more syllables are not treated.

2888.prule: Hedged weight-to-stress rule at word level (grammar §2.3.2.1-2.3.2.2, p. 63): every phonological word is minimally bimoraic and 'must have at least one primary stress'; 'only bimoraic or relatively heavier syllables can receive a primary stress'; bimoraic-or-bigger syllables (long vowel = two moras; long vowel + coda = three) 'tend to attract stress', monomoraic syllables (typically a short ə) 'tend not to attract stress'. Feet are 'predominantly iambic'; in sesquisyllables (ə-presyllable + heavy final) tone and prosodic prominence are always on the word-final major syllable ('disyllabic iamb', HL overview §5). Only lexemes can head a phonological word hosting the primary-stressed syllable; affixes and clitics cannot. No positional rule for words with more than one heavy syllable is visible in the excerpt; the lexicon is 'primarily' monosyllabic and polysyllables are 'typically' compounds.

2889.prule: Free (not bound to a position), mobile dynamic stress: in disyllables on either the first or the second syllable, lexically; polysyllables (a minority) tend toward final stress; no quantity or segmental condition stated.
2889.srule: Only in complex verb forms: two-component (periphrastic) verb forms have main stress on the lexical component and secondary stress on the auxiliary (r‘izȫ́ (h)ȍst 'he lay'); negated verbs have main stress on na- and secondary stress on the syllable stressed in the affirmative (ná-uzå̏(w)ō 'he did not stay'). 2898.prule: No stress-position rule is stated. The thesis describes a five-tone system and says only that polysyllabic words 'do not bear stress equally on every syllable': the unstressed syllable is reduced to an open short CV syllable carrying tone 3 only (the CVᵀ shape, which never occurs in monosyllables), and this reduced syllable is 'the first syllable of a 2-syllable word or the unstressed syllable of a polysyllabic word'. 2903.prule: Two lexically contrastive tones, high (marked /´/) and low (unmarked), with minimal pairs (duhíyá/duhíya, wąbę́/wą́bę́, okóró/okóro). Stress is not an independent parameter: 'high tone and stress occur simultaneously'; the FIRST high-toned syllable of the phonological word carries the somewhat stronger (primary) stress plus optional nucleus lengthening, and each later H syllable is a little higher in pitch than the preceding one. The word generally has one primary-stress syllable. Because the common word melodies are H, LH, LHL, LHH, LHLL, LHHH and initial-H melodies (HH, HL, HHL, HLL, HHH, HLLL) are rare, primary stress most often falls on the 2nd syllable, sometimes the 1st; the position is set by the lexical tone melody, not by syllable count or weight.
2903.srule: Every high-toned syllable carries stress ('El tono alto y el acento ocurren simultáneamente'); the first high-toned syllable has the slightly stronger main stress and optional lengthening, each later high-toned syllable a weaker stress at successively higher pitch (basáhá [bàA'sá'há], tíkóró ['tí'kó'řó]). Non-primary stresses thus fall on the later H syllables of the lexical melody (LHH, LHHH, HH...); words with a single H have one stress. Not rhythmic. Waltz & Waltz (Notas 2015: 5, 7-8) likewise allow 'acentos múltiples' in one phonological word, and Waltz 2012: 5 calls the stresses after the first 'secundarios'.

tn.quote: As a convention, I will call the Polci cluster ‘Polci’ and the Polci language ‘Po’. Po and Za are three-tone languages (Lo = à; Mid = a; Hi = á); the others are two-tone languages (Lo = à; Hi = a). This will make it difficult for the time being to mark tones on CP ... Abbreviations: ... Hi: High tone; ... Lo: Low tone; ... Mid: Middle tone; ... Ri: Rising tone ... SBW has lost gender and tends to express number through tone contrast. Polci has not taken that process as far as Za.
